title: Global insights on the impact of solar power plants on bird populations
abstract: Renewable energy sources, particularly solar power plants, have been increasingly widespread in recent decades. Due to the significant decrease in the cost of solar panels over the past twenty years, a rise in the number of photovoltaic installations is expected. This will lead to the formation and spread of a new type of anthropogenically transformed landscapes. Over the last decade, studies have been published evaluating the impact of solar power plants on soil cover, vegetation, wildlife, and specifically, bird fauna. These studies primarily focus on mortality factors, forecasting bird mortality as the total capacity and area of photovoltaic installations increase. Researchers conclude that the available data is insufficient to fully understand the complex interactions between the abiotic and biotic components of this new habitat. However, it is already well-established that bird mortality at solar energy facilities is the lowest compared to fossil fuel-based plants and other renewable energy sources. Some findings even suggest that photovoltaic installations may have a positive impact on biodiversity compared to other technogenically altered landscapes. Studies have documented various mechanisms through which solar power plants can affect bird populations. The physical presence of solar panels may disrupt flight routes and nesting sites. However, it is also noted that the reflective surfaces of photovoltaic panels can attract insects, which in turn provide new feeding opportunities for certain bird species. This paper aims to summarize the current global experience in assessing the impact of solar power plants on birds.

# **GLOBAL INSIGHTS ON THE IMPACT OF SOLAR POWER PLANTS ON BIRD POPULATIONS**

## **Review article**

## Yuzyk A. V.

_H.S. Skovoroda Kharkiv National Pedagogical University e-mail: andriyuzuk@gmail.com_

_https://doi.org/10.34142/2708-5848.2024.26.1.06_

Renewable energy sources, particularly solar power plants, have been increasingly widespread in recent decades. Due to the significant decrease in the cost of solar panels over the past twenty years, a rise in the number of photovoltaic installations is expected. This will lead to the formation and spread of a new type of anthropogenically transformed landscapes. Over the last decade, studies have been published evaluating the impact of solar power plants on soil cover, vegetation, wildlife, and specifically, bird fauna. These studies primarily focus on mortality factors, forecasting bird mortality as the total capacity and area of photovoltaic installations increase. Researchers conclude that the available data is insufficient to fully understand the complex interactions between the abiotic and biotic components of this new habitat. However, it is already well-established that bird mortality at solar energy facilities is the lowest compared to fossil fuelbased plants and other renewable energy sources. Some findings even suggest that photovoltaic installations may have a positive impact on biodiversity compared to other technogenically altered landscapes. Studies have documented various mechanisms through which solar power plants can affect bird populations. The physical presence of solar panels may disrupt flight routes and nesting sites. However, it is also noted that the reflective surfaces of photovoltaic panels can attract insects, which in turn provide new feeding opportunities for certain bird species. This paper aims to summarize the current global experience in assessing the impact of solar power plants on birds. _**Keywords:**_ biodiversity monitoring, birds, impact, mortality, solar energy, solar power plants.

Every year, the Sun emits significantly more energy to Earth than humanity uses. The planet receives over 2500 TW of solar energy available for technical use over large areas of its surface [53, 79]. In recent decades, alternative energy sources have been implemented, including solar power plants (SPP), which are divided into photovoltaic (PV) and concentrated solar power (CSP) based on their generation principles [25, 41]. As climate change is currently identified as the greatest threat to biodiversity conservation, particularly for birds [82], the implementation of solar power plants offers a sustainable solution to reduce reliance on fossil fuels and mitigate environmental impacts.

Solar power plants have become a new anthropogenic habitat, which will become more widespread over time. However, information on their impact on biodiversity is scarce and spatially limited [32]. The potential impact of SPP on birds includes habitat loss and mortality from collisions [69]. Industrial-

scale solar power plants require 2 to 5 hectares per megawatt of capacity [25], and in most cases, this involves complete vegetation removal [12, 44]. Moreover, the construction of SPP and other alternative sources raises concerns about wildlife habitat reduction and competition with food production for humans [10, 18, 44, 49, 58, 75]. This trend towards the degradation or fragmentation of natural areas is particularly concerning [44], especially for birds that are endangered, have limited ranges, and higher habitat requirements. For instance, the discovery of injured and dead waterbirds (Pelecaniformes, Gaviiformes, Podicipediformes) at specific SPP in the USA forced scientists to hypothesize that birds perceive large areas of SPP as water bodies (the "big lake effect") [23, 33, 69].

The area required for photovoltaic (PV) solar power plants depends on several factors: the latitude of the location (shading negatively affects generation, so in latitudes further from the equator, rows of panels need to be installed

with greater spacing, increasing the area required) and the efficiency of the solar panels (more efficient panels generate more power per unit area).

In 2022, the average efficiency of photovoltaic modules worldwide, according to the report by the U.S. National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), was 21-22%. The average efficiency of monocrystalline panels installed in the U.S. was 20.7% [19]. However, on December 18, 2023, LONGi Green Energy Technology Co., Ltd set a world record for the efficiency of silicon solar cells, certified by the Institute for Solar Energy Research in Hamelin, Germany (Institut für Solarenergieforschung GmbH), reaching a value of 27.09%.

Research at solar power plants in California (USA) has documented instances of bird mortality. Polarized light attracts insects, which in turn attract insectivorous birds, increasing the risk of collisions [29]. Different solar power plants will have varying impacts on avifauna in the areas where they are installed. This article aims to analyze the existing global experience in assessing the impact of solar power plants on birds.

## **MATERIALS AND METHODS**

The study focused on analyzing scientific works in the fields of renewable energy, ornithology, and ecology. Over 80 literature sources in electronic format from the past 50 years were analyzed, which related to the assessment of the impact of solar power plants on birds. In analyzing the literature sources, the main emphasis was placed on identifying the factors of both positive and negative impacts of SPP on birdlife, and on modern approaches

to protecting birds from the negative effects. When identifying information about the positive impact of SPP on birds, specific examples and mechanisms by which solar power plants contribute to the preservation and improvement of birdlife were analyzed, and the possibilities of applying these approaches in practice were considered.

## **RESULTS**

The author found research results on the impact of solar power plants on avifauna in the USA [24, 25, 26, 33, 41, 48], the Republic of South Africa [83], Europe, including the United Kingdom [21, 51, 76], Germany [57], Slovakia [32], Spain [26], Israel [26], and Japan [34].

The paradigm of using clean energy and reviews of its environmental impact began in the 1970s [22, 25, 46]. A. Lovins initiated the classification of energy sources on a scale from safe to harmful, based on the presence of waste and the environmental impact throughout the energy supply chain [46]. Quantitative studies on the impact of SPP on biodiversity and

comparisons of these areas with undisturbed natural areas in terms of biodiversity were rare until 2000 [48, 63]. There have been warnings that SPP could lead to biodiversity loss within areas under the plants and other infrastructure, such as power lines, due to vegetation removal, leveling of the topsoil, and landscape fragmentation, which create barriers for species movement and gene flow [62]. Later studies on bird mortality due to collisions with power lines or telecommunication towers confirmed this concern [15, 42, 58].

Two types of bird mortality have been identified at solar power plants: collisionrelated mortality, which is observed in all types

of solar power plants, and burn-related mortality caused by concentrated sunlight, which is specific to concentrated solar power (CSP) plants. The latter includes all injuries that result in either immediate death or burns that impair or diminish flight ability, making it difficult or impossible for birds to obtain food or protect themselves from predators [25, 33, 48].

The nature and scale of the impact of solar power plants on birds depend on a combination of three factors: location, type, and size [44]. Specifically, the risk of mortality increases when SPP are built near migration routes or wetlands [71], when engineering solutions attract birds, such as cooling ponds, and when the height of the solar power plant is increased [17, 20]. Additionally, SPP can attract insects, which in turn attract birds, further increasing the risk of bird collisions and mortality [29, 33, 44].

Given the insufficient empirical data, approaches to studying bird mortality risk rely on monitoring methods developed and applied to other structures, such as glass surfaces on high-rise buildings [14, 35], power lines [58], wind turbines or traditional energy facilities [16, 67, 72], and highways [43]. These methods provide a foundation for assessing and mitigating the risks associated with solar power plants, despite the unique challenges they present.

The standard metric for estimating bird mortality at energy facilities is the number of fatalities per year divided by the capacity of the facility (birds/MW/year or birds•MW[−1] •year[−1] ) or the number of fatalities divided by the gigawatt-hour of electricity generated (birds/GWh)  [16, 72]. However, the reliability of these estimates is influenced by both human and biological factors. Researchers' ability to cover the entire area of the SPP or a portion of it, their observational skills, the ability to detect carcasses in various terrains and among engineering structures all play a significant role. Additionally, the presence of scavengers that consume carcasses in the vicinity of the SPP further complicates mortality counts.. Therefore, mathematical approaches should be applied to adjust the monitoring results [30, 58, 65, 68].

Acoustic monitoring at solar power plants using acoustic receivers allows for automated recording of species diversity and reduces the labor intensity of the process [47, 85, 86, 87]. This method enables continuous and comprehensive data collection, providing valuable insights into the presence and behavior of bird species around solar power plants.

## **Global experience in studying the impact of concentrated solar power (CSP) plants on avifauna.**

The world’s first CSP plant, Solar One, began operation on April 12, 1982, in California, USA [37]. As of 2024, the largest operational CSP plant is the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, with a total capacity of 950 MW. This includes a 100 MW CSP plant with the world’s tallest solar receiver tower at 263 meters, a 600 MW parabolic trough complex, and a 250 MW PV station [13]. In the United States, the largest CSP plant is the Ivanpah Solar Power Facility with a capacity of 392 MW [40].

In the early 2010s, the global CSP capacity was about 1 GW, which increased to nearly 6.2 GW by the end of 2023. Leading countries in CSP installations are Spain with a total capacity of 2.3 GW, the USA (1.5 GW), China (596 MW), Morocco (533 MW), and South Africa (500 MW) [64].

_**The impact of the Solar One CSP on birds.**_ M. McCrary with co-authors conducted a study on bird mortality at Solar One between May and June 1982 (six visits lasting 2-3 days each) and from September 1982 to May 1983 (34 visits lasting 2-3 days each). The entire facility and surrounding areas were inspected. Over 40 weeks of observations, 70 bird deaths were recorded, involving 26 species. The causes of mortality were collisions with engineering structures (57 cases, 81%, 20 species), mainly parabolic mirrors (75% of collision-related deaths), and burns (13 cases, 19%, 7 species). A total of 107 bird species were identified in the areas adjacent to the CSP plant, most of which were migratory, with only 15 species being nesting birds. The diversity is associated with the presence of an artificial water body nearby. In contrast, the average

number of bird species in a similar natural desert environment in Arizona is only 20.

While this impact on local avifauna can be cautiously considered minimal, more powerful CSP plants with higher towers may pose greater risks. Therefore, it is advisable to locate them away from water bodies, agricultural lands, and habitats of rare and protected bird species [48].

_**The impact of the Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System on local avifauna.**_ C. Ho provides a comprehensive review of bird mortality data at various CSP plants: Solar One, the Solar Energy Development Center (SEDC) in Israel, Ivanpah, Crescent Dunes in Nevada, USA, and Gemasolar in Spain. The average bird mortality at Ivanpah ranges from 0.7 to 3.5 bird/GWh, which is lower than that at fossil fuel plants [26].

Documented cases of bird mortality due to high-intensity light burns have been reported at Ivanpah [24, 26, 33, 84]. In these instances, birds have been exposed to concentrated solar radiation exceeding safe limits. The safe solar radiation limits for birds are between 4 to 50 kW/m2 [26]. Exceeding these limits can result in fatal burns, highlighting the need for careful management and mitigation strategies at concentrated solar power facilities.

R. Kagan and colleagues observed bird mortality at Ivanpah due to intense solar flux, impact trauma, and predation. Of the 141 mortality cases, 47 (33%) had signs of burnt feathers, which incapacitated flight and led to death. No eye or tissue burns were observed [26, 33]. Thus, concentrated solar radiation can significantly harm local bird populations, highlighting the need for careful management of this aspect and implementation of impact mitigation strategies to preserve birds and their habitats.

C. Ho refuted the theory of complete combustion of birds exposed to concentrated solar flux. For complete combustion of birds weighing between 10 to 1000 g., the concentrated solar irradiance should be

between 4 to 20 MW/m2 with exposure times of 10 seconds, significantly higher than realworld figures (approximately 600 kW/m2 at Ivanpah CSP) [26]. The findings challenge the hypothesis of complete combustion of birds due to concentrated solar flux, suggesting realworld irradiance levels at facilities like Ivanpah CSP are insufficient to cause such extreme effects within the studied exposure parameters.

From October 29, 2013, to October 20, 2014, H. Harvey and colleagues conducted a detailed study of bird mortality at Ivanpah. They surveyed the energy tower and adjacent heliostats across 154 acres (100% surveyed), with sporadic surveys on the remaining 720 acres (24.1% surveyed). Over a year, 703 bird fatalities were recorded, including 25 injuries leading to death. Extrapolating these results, the estimated total mortality was 3504 cases, with known causes for 1492 cases (42.6%). Of these, 51.9% died from collisions, 47.4% from feather burns, and 0.7% from other causes, such as entrapment in cooling systems. Various researchers have documented the negative impact of this SCP on birds, thus necessitating the implementation of a series of measures to mitigate its adverse effects. That is why the plant has implemented advanced software to reduce heliostat upright time, insect-repellent LED lighting, anti-perching devices, and electronic bird deterrents [24, 26].

Bird mortality can be reduced by various deterrents: acoustic (imitation of distress or predator sounds), visual (mannequins, intense lighting), physical (spikes to prevent perching), and chemosensory (various chemical substances that deter birds, e.g., Methyl anthranilate). These measures have proven successful at Ivanpah CSP [24, 26].

_**The impact of the Solar Energy Development Center on birds and experiments to establish factors influencing birds.**_ In the Negev Desert, southern Israel, the Solar Energy Development Center (SEDC) is a 6 MW CSP plant with high receiver towers. No bird deaths were recorded as of 2016, despite surveys being conducted four times a

week along 20-meter transects [26].

The absence of documented bird mortality at this energy facility did not deter scientists from conducting a series of experiments to establish factors influencing birds. G. Santolo studied the impact of concentrated solar flux levels on bird carcasses at SEDC. He found that exposure to up to 50 kW/m2 for up to 30 seconds did not damage feathers or muscle tissues of the carcasses [26, 61].

Conversely, R. Tyler and colleagues determined that exposure to solar flux above 4 kW/m2 for 60 seconds raised wing temperatures to 160°C, leading to tissue destruction [7].

These studies indicate that two parameters have a significant impact on bird mortality on CSP. The first is the intensity of concentrated solar radiation. The second is the duration of exposure to this impact.

_**The impact of the Crescent Dunes CSP on local avifauna.**_ On January 14, 2015, a significant incident of bird mortality occurred at the Crescent Dunes CSP in Nevada, USA, which has a capacity of 110 MW. The incident was attributed to the concentration of heliostats at the solar flux convergence point above the receiver tower. Specifically, 115 birds were killed due to the intense solar flux at that focal point.

Following the dispersion of the solar flux to below 4 kW/m2, no further bird mortality was recorded at the plant [26, 55].

This incident underscores the critical importance of managing solar flux levels to mitigate bird fatalities at CSP plants. It also highlights the effectiveness of reducing solar flux intensity as a preventive measure against bird deaths.

_**Study of the impact of the Gemasolar SCP in Spain on birds.**_ Results of Dr. Pleguenzuelos from the University of Granada, Spain, on the Gemasolar CSP plant (Andalusia, Spain), with a capacity of 20 MW, show significant bird populations in the region, yet a 14-month study found no bird fatalities at the station [26]. These findings underscore the importance of continued monitoring and research to understand the long-term impacts of SCP on avian species.

_**Advancements in reducing bird mortality at CSP through technological innovations.**_ With the development of computer technologies, measures to reduce bird mortality at CSP plants have been enhanced. A methodology for assessing light beam hazard for birds was developed by combining mathematical models of heat exchange and irradiance in the airspace above the power station [27]. A mathematical model of bird feather temperature was developed to determine its dependence on solar irradiation, heliostat positioning time, and generation dynamics [27]. C. Sims and colleagues created the Tower Illuminance Model (TIM), allowing real-time interactive investigation of light reflection hazard for birds during flight and orientation in modeled space [66].

In conclusion, advancements in computer technologies have significantly improved efforts to mitigate bird mortality at CSP plants. The development of methodologies such as assessing light beam hazards and mathematical models for bird feather temperature dependency on solar irradiation and heliostat positioning demonstrate proactive approaches in understanding and minimizing the impact on avian species.

## **Global experience in studying the impact of photovoltaic (PV) solar power plants on avifauna.**

The following provides an overview of some of the world's largest solar power plants and their contributions to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The significant expansion of solar power plants around the globe highlights their crucial role in combating climate change. The world's largest as of 2024, the Bhadla Solar Park in India, with a capacity of 2245 MW, is expected to annually avoid 4 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions [2, 77]. In the USA, the largest PV plant is the Spotsilvania Solar PV Park in Virginia, with a total capacity of 617.9 MW, aiming to avoid 340,000 tons of CO2 emissions per year [59]. In Ukraine, solar energy has rapidly developed before the russian invasion, ranking among the top ten leaders in Europe. The largest industrial PV plant with a capacity of 240 MW is located near the village of Pokrovske in the Nikopol

district of the Dnipropetrovsk region, expected to avoid 420,000 tons of CO2 emissions per year [78].

In 2010, the total capacity of all PV stations in the USA was 900 MW and doubled within a year [25]. Globally, PV capacity was nearly 50 GW in 2010, rising to over 650 GW by 2020, with a projected capacity of 1600 GW by 2030. In the European Union, PV capacity was nearly 90 GW in 2015, doubling compared to 2010. In 2020, the world leaders were China (204.7 GW), the European Union (131.3 GW), the USA (75.9 GW), Japan (63 GW), and India (42.8 GW), with a total capacity of 517.7 GW [31, 50]. This remarkable growth trajectory underscores the increasing reliance on solar energy as a key component in the global shift towards sustainable energy solutions. However, as the total capacity of solar power plants increases, so does the still poorly understood impact on living organisms, particularly avifauna.

Reviews on the ecological impact of solar energy installations on the environment are emerging [9, 44, 56, 80]. Constructing PV systems in existing built environments such as roofs and walls of buildings is considered the most environmentally friendly in terms of biodiversity conservation and environmental protection [11, 86]. Integrating installations into existing architectural and engineering elements, among other benefits, helps conserve natural habitats and minimize negative impacts on birds by installing many small-scale installations, which is permissible in many countries worldwide [73, 70, 88]. Photovoltaic PV systems are the safest for people and biodiversity among all alternative energy sources, including for civil aviation [4]. The integration of photovoltaic systems into existing structures presents a promising solution for expanding solar energy capacity while minimizing ecological impacts and preserving biodiversity.

Scientists conclude that on a global scale, the issue is currently under-researched and additional studies and data are needed to better understand the impacts of PV power

stations on birds [32, 41]. A negative trend is observed that with the increase in the capacity and size of PV power stations, the risks to birds, mainly mortality factors, increase [25, 33, 41]. Overall, further research is crucial to fully understand the impacts of PV power stations on birds, as increasing capacity and size of these installations correlate with higher risks to avian populations.

Shedding light on the insufficiently studied impact of solar power plants on birds and creating a foundation for further research can be aided by some existing studies.

_**Assessing avian mortality at photovoltaic Utility-scale solar energy projects in the U. S.**_ L. Walston and co-authors first analyzed bird mortality at regional (Southern California) and national (USA) scales based on data from three Utility-scale solar energy (USSE) projects in Southern California, one of which (the California Valley Solar Ranch (CVSR)) is an operational PV project with the electrical capacity of 250 MW [8]. It was found that annually in the region, between 16,200 and 59,400 birds die due to reasons associated with USSE (2.7 birds/MW/year), mortality from unknown causes (7.3 birds/MW/year), and overall mortality (9.5 birds/MW/year). The total extrapolated to the scale of the USA mortality on established and under-construction projects is estimated to be between 37,800 and 138,600 birds per year [36, 41]. The analysis by L. Walston and colleagues underscores significant bird mortality associated with utility-scale solar energy projects in Southern California, highlighting the need for further research and mitigation strategies to minimize impacts on avian populations in the U. S. H. Harvey and co-authors provide the following data for CVSR considering a capacity factor of 30%: mortality rate associated with PV stations is 0.50 birds/MW/year or 0.23 birds/GWh; mortality rate from unknown causes is 10.20 birds/MW/year or 3.89 birds/GWh; overall mortality rate is 10.70 and 4.08, respectively [23, 41]. The findings presented by H. Harvey

and colleagues highlight varying mortality rates at the CVSR, underscoring the complex dynamics of bird fatalities linked to photovoltaic stations, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive monitoring and mitigation strategies in solar energy development.

Studies of bird mortality at PV USSE projects in the Southwestern U. S. conducted from November 2013 to September 2018 identified 669 bird fatalities across 86 species. Songbirds (Passeriformes) and pigeons and doves (Columbiformes) were most frequently affected (243 and 183 number of detections, respectively). Mortality detections varied among different USSE projects from 0.08 birds/MW/year to 9.26 birds/MW/year, with an average of 1.82 birds/MW/year or 10,920 detections per year for the Southwestern U. S. [36], which is lower than previous studies in this region [41].

The research into bird mortality at photovoltaic USSE projects in the U. S. underscores significant variability in mortality rates across projects The findings emphasize the need for tailored mitigation strategies to minimize bird fatalities in solar energy development.

_**Assessing avian mortality at photovoltaic Utility-scale solar energy project in the the Republic of South Africa.**_ The largest PV power plant in the Northern Cape province of the Republic of South Africa (180 ha, 96 MW) did not impact any endangered bird species. It registered 38 species with a density of 1.80±0.50 birds/ha, which are lower values compared to adjacent undisturbed areas (47 species, 2.57±0.86 birds/ha). Over a 3- month observation period, 8 mortality cases due to collision with solar panels were recorded, extrapolating to 435 birds per year (4.5 birds/MW/year) [83]. The study conducted at the largest PV power plant in South Africa's Northern Cape province indicates minimal impact on endangered bird species, with observed bird densities lower than adjacent undisturbed areas. Despite recording a few collision-related mortalities, the overall impact on bird populations remains relatively low, suggesting effective mitigation measures could further minimize risks

associated with solar panel collisions.

## _**Enhancing avian biodiversity: the impact of photovoltaic solar power plants and studies from Europe.**_

Regarding the impact of PV solar power plants on birds, the presence of engineering structures not only acts as a mortality factor but also provides nesting opportunities and shelters from summer heat, and attracts insects over the stations, which can positively influence local avifauna [12, 80, 85]. This view is supported by studies from Slovakia, including the Western Carpathians [32].  It has been found that photovoltaic solar power plants alter the plant species composition underneath the constructions [39] through shading and moisture retention [54]. This supports a higher invertebrate [5] and avian species diversity, makes microenvironments more complex and heterogeneous, creates nesting sites, and protects against predatory birds [54].  Furthermore, the SPP are designed for electricity production. Future development with an emphasis on biodiversity conservation could have an even greater positive impact [32, 57]. Photovoltaic solar power plants can positively influence local bird populations by providing nesting opportunities, altering plant species composition, and supporting higher biodiversity through shading and moisture retention.

In Europe, there is a trend of declining breeding bird populations, particularly insectivorous species [6], due to various factors [74], including the use of pesticides [52]. Within photovoltaic SPP, higher numbers and species diversity of birds have been recorded compared to control plots in other agricultural lands (pastures, arable lands): 353 detections across 41 species, compared to 271 detections across 40 species. The most frequently observed species within the PV SPP were: Black Redstart ( _Phoenicurus ochruros_ Gmelin, 1774), White Wagtail ( _Motacilla alba_ L., 1758), Red-backed Shrike ( _Lanius collurio_ L., 1758), the European Stonechat ( _Saxicola rubicola_ L., 1766), and the Eurasian Tree Sparrow ( _Passer montanus_ L., 1758), which were identified as indicator species. Comparing faunas revealed the greatest differences between PV SPP and fallow lands.

Most of the species found within PV SPP supplement their diet or feed their nestlings with insects, hence the plants' greatest positive impact occurs during the breeding season [32]. It can also be hypothesized that PV power plants provide a positive impact on agricultural bird fauna during other seasons, as sites for foraging, roosting during wintering or migrations [60]. Photovoltaic solar power plants support higher bird species diversity and numbers compared to other agricultural lands, particularly benefiting insectivorous species. These plants provide crucial habitats for breeding, foraging, and roosting, contributing positively to bird populations throughout the year.

The results are consistent with studies in the United Kingdom [51] and Germany [57], where it has been found that species diversity and bird abundance at PV SPP are higher than on adjacent non-built anthropogenic lands. However, in Japan, bird species diversity at PV SPP did not differ from agricultural and wetland areas and was lower than temporarily non-cultivated lands [34]. In the United Kingdom and Germany, PV SPP installations are considered conservation measures to increase biodiversity on anthropogenically transformed landscapes [3, 21, 51, 57, 76], including the installation of artificial nesting sites [57]. Studies from the United Kingdom and Germany show that PV solar power plants enhance bird diversity and abundance, while in Japan, such benefits are not observed, highlighting regional differences in the impact of these installations on avian populations.

## **CONCLUSIONS**

Based on the analysis of a range of literature regarding the impact of solar power plants on avifauna, the following conclusions can be drawn:

1. The global expansion of solar energy demands the allocation of large land areas for plant installations, resulting in significant anthropogenic transformation and landscape fragmentation [12, 25, 44]. For PV SPP, one of the key factors is the efficiency of

solar panels. However, such energy installations substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions [1, 2]. A solution to this problem is decentralized generation through the installation of small-scale PV systems on rooftops and walls of existing buildings. This approach is relevant for biodiversity conservation, particularly avifauna [11, 41, 85], and as a means of countering armed aggression and energy terror in the context of full-scale invasion in Ukraine.

2. The impact of PV SPP on avifauna has been insufficiently researched and requires further research, especially at the regional level, as bird abundance, species composition, and activity vary across different territories [38, 72, 84].

3. The species composition of birds on technogenically transformed territories under USSE projects is less diverse compared to adjacent unchanged territories [12, 83], with exceptions found in certain concentrated CSP facilities located in the California desert with cooling ponds [48]. Species diversity at PV SPP is richer compared to other anthropogenic-transformed landscapes such as agricultural lands [32].

4. Mortality rates of birds at PV USSE are significantly lower compared to other anthropogenic territories and objects such as highways, communication towers, buildings, or traditional energy sources [15, 26, 41, 72]. At the same time, bird mortality is lower at PV SPP than at CSP facilities, which is due to the lack of a power tower of significant height and light flux concentration, the safe limits of which vary between 4-50 kW/m[2] [26].

5. The nature and scale of the impact on birds depend on the combination of three factors: the location of the SPP, its type, and size [44]. Negative impacts on avifauna increase sharply with the size and power of USSE projects, their spatial height, and the presence of nearby water bodies [17, 20, 41]. One factor is the polarization of light above PV SPP, which attracts insects and insectivorous birds [29]. Reducing mortality is achieved by

constructing USSE objects far from bird migration routes, wetlands, agricultural lands [17, 71], implementing various technical solutions such as acoustic, visual, tactile, and

chemosensory means to deter birds from installations [24], and developing mathematical models and improved software for CSP facilities [27, 28, 66].

## **УДК 504:620:598.2**

## **СВІТОВИЙ ДОСВІД ОЦІНКИ ВПЛИВУ СОНЯЧНИХ ЕЛЕКТРОСТАНЦІЙ НА ПТАХІВ**

## _Юзик А.В._

Відновлювані джерела енергії, зокрема, й сонячні електростанції, в останні десятиліття набувають все більшого поширення. У зв’язку із значним зниженням собівартості сонячних панелей за останні два десятиліття, можна очікувати збльшення кількості фотоелектричних установок. Це призведе до формування і поширення нового виду антропогенно-трансформованих ландшафтів. За останнє десятиліття були опубліковані роботи, присвячені оцінці впливу сонячних електростанцій на ґрунтовий покрив, рослинність, тваринний світ, зокрема, орнітофауну. Основний акцент у цих дослідженях робиться на факторі загибелі із прогнозуванням пташиної смертності у міру збільшення сумарної потужності та площі фотоелектричних установок.  Дослідники доходять висновку про недостатність наявних даних для розуміння повної картини всіх складних взаємовз’язків між абіотичним та біотичним складовими цього нового середовища існування. Станом на сьогодні вже достеменно відомо, що смертність птахів на об’єктах сонячної енергетики є найнижчою у порівнянні як із об’єктами, що працюють на викопному паливі, так і на інших джерелах відновлюваної енергії. Деякі результати свідчать навіть про позитивний вплив фотоелектричних установок на біорізноманіття, у порівнянні із іншими техногеннотрансформованими ландшафтами. Дослідження задокументували різні механізми, за допомогою яких сонячні електростанції можуть впливати на популяції птахів. Фізична присутність сонячних панелей може порушити маршрути польоту та місця гніздування. Однак також зазначається, що відбиваючі поверхні фотоелектричних панелей можуть приваблювати комах, що, у свою чергу, надає нові можливості для годування деяких видів птахів. Узагальнити наявну на даний час інформацію про світовий досвід оцінки впливу сонячних електростанцій на птахів й покликана дана робота.

_**Ключові слова**_ **:** сонячна енергія, сонячні електростанції, птахи, вплив, смертність, моніторинг біорізноманіття.
